text: Lessons 12 and 13 built and tested a failover group, but used geo-replication as its foundation without explaining the mechanism itself. Active geo-replication continuously copies transactions from the primary to a readable secondary in another region — the data-movement engine underneath the failover group's endpoint management.

It's asynchronous: the primary acknowledges a write to the application before confirming the secondary has received it. Synchronous replication would add real latency to every transaction by waiting for a distant secondary. That small lag window is exactly why Lesson 11 set RPO at 5 minutes rather than 0 — an explicit acknowledgment of asynchronous replication's cost.

The secondary lives in a genuinely different region so a region-wide outage doesn't take down both copies at once. And it's not purely a DR cost — in normal operation it can serve read-only reporting traffic, offloading load from the primary, which is worth mentioning when this platform's cost gets presented to leadership.

Next lesson pulls everything from this chapter — RPO and RTO targets, the failover group, the test results, and geo-replication's trade-offs — into a real DR runbook someone else could actually follow.
